{{Short description|Method used to estimate an individual's basal metabolic rate}}
The '''Harris–Benedict equation''' (also called the '''Harris-Benedict principle''') is a method used to estimate an individual's [[basal metabolic rate]] (BMR).<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Luy|first=Sybil Claudine|date=2018|title=Comparison of the Harris-Benedict Equation, Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis, and Indirect Calorimetry|journal=Journal of the ASEAN Federation of Endocrine Societies|volume=33|issue=2|pages=152–159|doi=10.15605/jafes.033.02.07|issn=0857-1074|pmc=7784146|pmid=33442121}}</ref>

The estimated BMR value may be multiplied by a number that corresponds to the individual's activity level; the resulting number is the approximate daily [[kilocalorie]] intake to maintain current [[body weight]].

The Harris-Benedict equation may be used to assist weight loss — by reducing the kilocalorie intake number below the estimated maintenance intake of the equation.{{citation needed|date=September 2014}}

== Calculating the Harris-Benedict BMR ==
The original Harris–Benedict equations were published in 1918 and 1919.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Harris JA, Benedict FG |title=A Biometric Study of Human Basal Metabolism |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=4 |issue=12 |pages=370–3 |year=1918 |pmid=16576330 |pmc=1091498 |doi=10.1073/pnas.4.12.370|bibcode=1918PNAS....4..370H |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>[https://archive.org/details/biometricstudyof00harruoft ''A Biometric Study of Basal Metabolism in Man'']. J. Arthur Harris and Francis G. Benedict. Washington, DC: Carnegie Institution, 1919.</ref>

{| class="wikitable"
|-
! Sex !! Calculations of BMR
|-
| Male
| <math>{BMR}={a_m}M+{b_m}H-{c_m}T+d_m</math>
|-
| Female
| <math>{BMR}={a_f}M+{b_f}H-{c_f}T+d_f</math>

where M is the subject's mass, H is the subject's height, T is the subject's age, <math>a_m=13.7516 {kg}^{-1} {kcal}\ d^{-1}</math>, <math>b_m = 5.0033 {cm}^{-1} {kcal}\ d^{-1}</math>, <math>c_m=6.755 {kcal}\ a^{-1} d^{-1}</math>, <math>d_m=66.473 {kcal}\ d^{-1}</math>, <math>a_f=9.5634 {kg}^{-1} {kcal}\ d^{-1}</math>, <math>b_f = 1.8496 {cm}^{-1} {kcal}\ d^{-1}</math>, <math>c_f=4.6756 {kcal}\ a^{-1} d^{-1}</math>, and <math>d_f=655.0955 {kcal}\ d^{-1}</math>.

The coefficients were revised by Roza and Shizgal in 1984.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Roza AM, Shizgal HM |title=The Harris Benedict equation reevaluated: resting energy requirements and the body cell mass |journal=The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition |volume=40 |issue=1 |pages=168–82 |year=1984 |pmid=6741850 |url=http://www.ajcn.org/cgi/pmidlookup?view=long&pmid=6741850 |doi=10.1093/ajcn/40.1.168|doi-access=free |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==History==
The Harris-Benedict equation sprang from a study by [[James Arthur Harris]] and [[Francis Gano Benedict]], which was published in 1919 by the [[Carnegie Institution for Science|Carnegie Institution of Washington]] in the [[monograph]] [https://archive.org/details/biometricstudyof00harruoft A Biometric Study Of Basal Metabolism In Man].  A 1984 [[Basal metabolic rate|revision]] improved its accuracy. Mifflin et al. published an equation more predictive for modern lifestyles in 1990.<ref name=pmid2305711/> Later work produced BMR estimators that accounted for lean body mass.

==Issues in dietary use==
As the BMR equations do not attempt to take into account body composition, identical results can be calculated for a very muscular person, and an overweight person, who are both the same height, weight, age and gender. As muscle and fat require differing amounts of calories to maintain, the TEE estimates will not be accurate for such cases.

The paper behind the latest update (Mifflin et al) to the BMR formula states all participants in their study fall within the 'normal' and 'overweight' [[body mass index]] (BMI) categories, and so the results also do not necessarily apply to those in the 'underweight' or 'obese' BMI categories.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pavlidou |first=Eleni |date=2023-01-28 |title=Revised Harris-Benedict Equation: New Human Resting Metabolic Rate Equation |journal=Metabolites |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=189 |doi=10.3390/metabo13020189 |issn=2218-1989 |pmc=9967803 |pmid=36837808 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
